companyCaseStudy.title: How Netflix Cut Bandwidth by ~30% and Kept 200M+ Viewers Happy: Open Connect + Per‑Title Encoding at Planetary Scale
companyCaseStudy.summary: Netflix serves 200M+ subscribers across ~190 countries and routinely pushes many terabits/sec of video. To cut transit costs, reduce startup latency, and improve quality on bad networks, Netflix built Open Connect (their own CDN) and pioneered Per‑Title Encode + ABR optimizations — saving tens of millions in bandwidth and reducing average bitrate by roughly 20–40% while improving startup times.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook: video at planet scale

When your product is streaming video to >200 million subscribers across ~190 countries, every extra kilobit per second multiplies into huge monthly bills. Netflix faced two painful realities: internet transit was expensive and variable, and users abandoned streams that took too long to start or rebuffered. The stakes: multi‑Tbps of egress, tight startup-time SLAs (seconds matter), and razor-thin margins on encoding decisions.

## Problem → Challenge

- Problem: Deliver high-quality video globally with predictable cost and low startup latency.
- Challenges: ISP networks differ wildly; transit costs scale linearly with bandwidth; one-size-fits-all encoding wastes bits on easy titles or delivers insufficient quality on hard titles; caching efficiency matters — miss rates directly increase egress.

Key metrics Netflix needed to improve:

| Metric | Pain (Before) |
|--------|---------------|
| Global egress | Multiple Tbps of transit costs (growing with subscribers) |
| Startup latency | Seconds-level startup led to churn |
| Average bitrate | Overprovisioned for many titles = wasted bandwidth |
| Cache hit rate at edge | Lower hit rate => higher origin pulls and cost |


## The Decision: Build your own CDN + smarter encoding

Netflix pursued two complementary engineering plays:

1. Open Connect (their own CDN): deploy Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) inside ISP networks and at major IXPs so most viewer requests are satisfied locally instead of transiting expensive upstream providers.
2. Per‑Title Encode Optimization + Adaptive Bitrate (ABR): analyze each title to produce a custom encoding ladder (bitrate vs. resolution) that achieves target perceptual quality with the smallest bitrate, and pair with a client ABR algorithm that ramps startup quickly and adapts smoothly.

Why both? A smarter encode reduces bytes for every viewer; edge caches (OCAs) ensure those bytes are served over the cheapest, fastest path.

## Architecture (visual)

```mermaid
graph LR
  Viewer[Viewer (mobile/TV/PC)] -->|HTTPs + HLS/DASH| ISP[ISP Network]
  ISP -->|Peering| OCA[Open Connect Appliance (Edge Cache)]
  OCA -->|Cache miss| Regional[Regional Origin / Netflix POP]
  Regional --> Origin[Central Origin / S3-like Storage]

  subgraph EncodingPipeline
    ContentRepo[Source Files] --> Transcode[Per‑Title Multi‑rate Transcoder]
    Transcode --> Packager[HLS/DASH Packager]
    Packager --> Origin
  end

  ABR[Client ABR Logic] -. adapts .-> Viewer
  ABR -. telemetry .-> Metrics[Atlas + Mantis]
  Metrics -->|feed| Transcode
```

### Notes on architectural choices

- OCAs are standard HTTP caches built to be deployed inside ISP networks or at IXPs. They hold popular titles and serve byte ranges for HLS/DASH segments.
- Per‑Title Encode runs an analysis pass per title: some titles (animation/static scenes) compress far better than high-motion films. Netflix generates a custom ladder to minimize bitrate for a given perceptual quality target.
- Client-side ABR prioritizes quick startup (aggressive first-chunk selection) and then smooth ramp to the quality ladder point suited to measured throughput.
- Monitoring/telemetry (Netflix Atlas, Mantis, and event pipelines) feed back popularity and QoE signals to caching/encoding decisions.

## Implementation details & tradeoffs

- Prepositioning: OCAs are populated proactively for expected popular content (new releases, regional hits) and lazily for long-tail content.
- TTL and cache heuristics: Short TTLs for fresher assets (catalog changes), long TTLs for stable VOD chunks. Popularity drives aggressive replication.
- Encoding CPU vs. storage: Per‑Title Encode increases transcoding compute, but reduces network egress and storage-transfer costs. Netflix accepted higher offline CPU cost for lower ongoing bandwidth expense.
- ABR and chunk sizing: Small initial chunks (e.g., 2s) reduce startup time but increase request rate — OCAs and HTTP/2 keep request overhead manageable.

## Results (real, public engineering outcomes)

| Metric | Before | After (Open Connect + Per‑Title) |
|--------|--------|----------------------------------|
| Average bitrate per stream | Baseline | ~20–40% lower on many titles (Netlix TechBlog reported sizeable savings) |
| Edge offload | Significant transit dependence | Majority of Netflix traffic served from OCAs in many ISPs (often >80% locally) |
| Startup latency | Multiple seconds for warm streams | Reduced to ~1s regionally for many clients (aggressive ABR + OCA proximity) |
| Cost impact | High variable transit costs | Tens of millions saved annually (bandwidth savings × scale) |

Concrete public takeaways Netflix published:
- Per‑Title Encode delivers large bitrate savings while preserving perceptual quality (Netflix TechBlog). The technique decreased average required bitrate for many titles by roughly 20–40% depending on content.
- Open Connect offloads the vast majority of viewer traffic to appliances inside ISP networks and greatly reduces dependency on transit providers.

## Why it worked (and what to watch out for)

- Leverage locality: putting caches inside ISPs cuts latency and transit hops; many viewers benefit from the nearest OCA instead of a distant origin.
- Optimize per workload: one-size-fits-all encoding wastes bandwidth; per‑title analysis is more accurate and economical.
- Telemetry-driven ops: real-time metrics let Netflix spot unpopular prefetches, re-balance OCAs, and tune ABR parameters.

Caveats:
- OCA deployment requires coordination with ISPs and peering/placement engineering.
- Per‑Title Encode increases offline compute and complexity in the encoding pipeline.
- Edge cache correctness and cache consistency (e.g., content updates) require careful versioning/TTL strategies.

## Practical checklist if you want to copy parts of this approach

- Measure: gather baseline startup times, average bitrate per user, and your transit cost per Gbps.
- Start small: deploy edge caches in top ISPs/POPs and measure offload.
- Test per‑title encoding on a sample catalog; compare objective and perceptual quality vs bitrate.
- Integrate telemetry: route QoE and cache-hit signals back into placement and encode decisions.

## TL;DR — impact in one line

By combining Open Connect (edge appliances inside ISPs) with Per‑Title Encode + smart ABR, Netflix reduced the average bits sent per stream by ~20–40% for many titles, offloaded the majority of traffic to local caches, reduced startup latency to roughly ~1s for many viewers, and materially cut transit costs at planet scale.
keyTakeaways: Push content into the network: edge caches inside ISPs dramatically lower latency and transit egress (in many ISPs >80% of traffic served locally).
Optimize for the content: per‑title encode can reduce average bitrate ~20–40% while maintaining perceptual quality — trade extra offline CPU for ongoing bandwidth savings.
Telemetry is mandatory: continuous QoE and cache metrics close the loop between encoding, caching, and client ABR to keep systems optimized at scale.
relatedTopics: Adaptive bitrate streaming (ABR) and encoding optimization

concept.title: Cache Smarter, Not Harder: Write‑Through, Write‑Back, and Cache‑Aside Explained
concept.summary: Caching can make your app feel instant and reduce backend load — but the wrong caching strategy introduces stale data, bugs, and complexity. This guide explains the three most common cache patterns (cache-aside, write-through, write-back), when to use each, and pitfalls to avoid.
concept.explanation:
## WHY it matters

Databases are slow(er) and more expensive than memory. A well-placed cache can cut latency from hundreds of milliseconds to single-digit milliseconds and reduce DB load by orders of magnitude. But caching isn't magic — pick the wrong strategy and you get stale reads, lost writes, and subtle bugs.

**Analogy:** Think of your cache like a mini-fridge next to a pantry (the DB). A cache lets you grab a snack fast — but you must decide who puts groceries into the fridge and when. Do you always stock it when buying groceries (write-through)? Do you stash things in the fridge and update the pantry later (write-back)? Or do you only fetch into the fridge when you're hungry (cache-aside)?

---

## The three patterns (high-level)

- **Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)**: App checks the cache first; on a miss it loads from DB, puts the value in cache, and returns it. Writes go to the DB, and usually invalidate or update the cache.
- **Write-Through**: App writes to cache and cache synchronously writes to DB. Reads always check cache.
- **Write-Back (Write-Behind)**: App writes to cache; the cache acknowledges immediately and asynchronously flushes writes to the DB later.


### Mermaid: Cache-Aside (flow)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Client Request] --> Cache{Cache Lookup}
  Cache -- Hit --> Return[Return Cached Value]
  Cache -- Miss --> DB[Read from DB]
  DB --> CacheStore[Store in Cache]
  CacheStore --> Return[Return Value]
```

### Mermaid: Write-Through (sequence)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Service: PUT key,value
  Service->>Cache: Set key,value
  Cache->>DB: Synchronously write key,value
  DB-->>Cache: Ack
  Cache-->>Service: Ack
  Service-->>Client: Success
```

---

## BEFORE / AFTER example (typical effect)

| Metric | Before (no cache) | After (cache hit rate 90%) |
|--------|-------------------:|---------------------------:|
| Avg read latency | 120 ms | 8 ms |
| DB read QPS | 10,000 | 1,000 |
| Cost per read (infra) | High | Much lower |

Note: benefits depend on hit rate, object size, and eviction behavior.

---

## Comparison: Pros / Cons / When to use

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| Cache-Aside | Simple, explicit control, no special cache code required | Must manage cache invalidation; potential thundering herd on cold keys | Read-heavy, eventually-consistent workloads; simple deployments
| Write-Through | Stronger read consistency (cache reflects latest writes), simpler reads | Write latency includes DB write; higher write amplification | When reads must reflect recent writes and write QPS is moderate
| Write-Back | Fast writes (low latency) and reduced DB write amplification | Risk of data loss on cache failure; complex flush logic; warm-up cost | High write-throughput use cases that can tolerate eventual durability (with strong guarantees)

---

## Practical examples and code

### 1) Cache-Aside (typical read path)

Use when reads are much more frequent than writes and stale reads for a short window are acceptable.

```python
# Python + redis (simplified)
import redis
r = redis.Redis()

def get_user(user_id):
    key = f"user:{user_id}"
    data = r.get(key)
    if data:
        return deserialize(data)
    # cache miss -> load from DB
    user = db.fetch_user(user_id)
    if user:
        r.set(key, serialize(user), ex=300)  # TTL 5m
    return user

def update_user(user_id, new_data):
    db.update_user(user_id, new_data)
    r.delete(f"user:{user_id}")  # invalidate cache
```

Pitfalls: stale reads during the small window between DB write and cache invalidation; thundering herd on popular cold keys.

### 2) Write-Through

Writes synchronously persist to cache and DB.

```js
// Node.js pseudo-code
async function put(key, value) {
  await cache.set(key, value);           // fast in-memory
  await db.write(key, value);            // synchronous durability
  return true;
}
```

This keeps reads simple and consistent, but write latency includes DB round-trip.

### 3) Write-Back (Write-Behind)

Writes are accepted by cache immediately; the cache flushes to DB in the background.

```text
Client -> Cache (ack immediately)
Cache holds dirty entry -> Background flusher batches writes -> DB
```

Pitfalls: data loss if cache crashes before flush; complexity around ordering, batching, and crash recovery. Use only with durable queueing or when cache is backed by a persistent log.

---

## Operational concerns & common pitfalls

- *Stale data / consistency*: For strong consistency, write-through (or synchronous DB writes) is safer. If you use cache-aside, ensure invalidation is correct and atomic relative to DB updates.
- *Thundering herd*: On a cold key, many requests may hit DB. Mitigate with locking or singleflight (coalescing), or pre-warming popular keys.
- *Cache evictions*: Evicted hot keys cause sudden DB spikes. Monitor evictions and adjust TTLs or memory.
- *Data loss with write-back*: If the cache fails before flushing, writes can be lost. Add replication, persistence, or a write-ahead log.
- *Complexity trade-offs*: Write-back reduces DB writes but increases operational complexity. Prefer simpler patterns unless you need the throughput.

---

## Quick checklist for choosing a strategy

1. Do reads dominate and can be slightly stale? -> Cache-Aside.
2. Do reads need to reflect latest writes and writes QPS is moderate? -> Write-Through.
3. Do you need ultra-low write latency and can accept complex operations and risk? -> Write-Back (only with safeguards).

---

## When caching breaks (and how to detect)

- Sudden spike in DB QPS after a deploy -> cache invalidation bug.
- Elevated cache evictions -> memory pressure or bad key sizing.
- Increased error rate on writes -> backlog or flusher issues (write-back).

Monitoring: cache hit/miss ratio, evictions/sec, TTL distributions, and write backlog size.

---

## Final analogy recap

Treat the cache like a mini-fridge: keep frequently used items close, decide who restocks, and have a plan if the fridge breaks. The right strategy depends on freshness needs, write volume, and how much operational complexity you can tolerate.
keyTakeaways: Cache-aside is simple and common for read-heavy workloads but requires careful invalidation.
Write-through gives fresher reads at the cost of write latency and DB load.
Write-back offers low write latency but increases risk and operational complexity — use only with strong durability safeguards.
